title: Looking for a few people interested in building a small ML trading research project
author: Remarkable_Race5767
selftext:
I’m looking to connect with a few people who are interested in building and learning through a small machine-learning trading research project together.

The focus is on market data, strategy research, careful backtesting, risk controls, and paper trading first—no real-money trading, profit promises, or paid positions.

You do not have to be an expert. If you have experience or interest in Python, ML, quantitative research, data, backtesting, or risk management, feel free to comment or send me a message with what you enjoy working on.

comments.author: d1jpd01
comments.body: I’m interested.  I have some questions, can I DM you?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The part that decides whether this works is not the modelling, it is whoever volunteers to own the data. Splits, delistings and point in time fundamentals eat most of the calendar and nobody wants that job, so groups like this drift toward notebooks built on whatever csv was handy.

Pick the universe and the adjustment rules before anyone trains anything, and write down the day you froze them.

replies.author: Remarkable_Race5767
replies.body:
That makes a lot of sense, and I appreciate you calling it out. We definitely do not want to build models on whatever CSV happens to be available and then mistake the results for real evidence.

Before anyone trains anything, we’ll define and document:

\- The initial asset universe  
\- The data source and timeframes  
\- How splits, delistings, missing data, and corporate actions are handled  
\- The point-in-time rules for any fundamentals or features  
\- The date/version when those assumptions are frozen

Data ownership and reproducibility should be a real workstream, not an afterthought. If you have a practical starting framework or checklist for setting that up properly, I’d genuinely appreciate your perspective.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Point in time is the one to settle first, the rest of that list is downstream of it. Cheapest version that works: store the as-of date beside every row and make the loader refuse anything dated later than the bar it's serving. Do that before you pick the universe, not after.

replies.author: Remarkable_Race5767
replies.body:
That is a helpful distinction, Thank you. We’ll treat point in time integrity as the first data requirement, before choosing the initial universe or training any models.

We’ll store an explicit as-of/availability timestamp with each data record and make the research loader reject data whose availability time is later than the decision bar being evaluated. We’ll also document the exact timing convention and test it before building features.

If you have recommendations on a minimal schema or a test case that reliably catches common point-in-time leakage, I’d appreciate them.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
One thing an as-of stamp on the row will not catch: split and dividend adjustments get applied backwards through the whole price history. The row keeps its original timestamp while the values underneath quietly change.

Same trap in the universe file. Delisted tickers drop off today's list and the backtest never sees them.

replies.author: Remarkable_Race5767
replies.body:
That’s an important catch thank you. An availability timestamp alone is not enough if our vendor rewrites historical values after splits or dividends, or if a current universe excludes securities that later delisted.

We’ll need to preserve versioned/raw data snapshots, clearly document whether prices are unadjusted or adjusted, and apply corporate-action adjustments according to the information available at each historical decision point. We’ll also use a point-in-time universe that retains delisted securities rather than relying on a present-day ticker list.

For an initial paper-trading project, would you recommend beginning with unadjusted daily bars plus a separate, versioned corporate-actions table—or is there a simpler minimum setup you consider safe enough for learning?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Cheapest test for the rewriting problem: pick a fixed past date, pull the same window from the vendor once a week, and diff it against last week's pull. Inside a month you know whether they rewrite and which fields move.

Costs almost nothing and it beats trusting their changelog.

replies.author: Remarkable_Race5767
replies.body:
That is a great practical test—thank you. We can treat the repeated pulls as an audit trail instead of assuming historical data stays fixed.

We’ll choose a fixed historical window, snapshot the same vendor pull on a regular schedule, and automatically diff it against the prior snapshot by ticker, date, and field. That should tell us whether revisions are happening and help us make the adjustment policy explicit before trusting any backtest.

Really appreciate the concrete suggestion.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
if you diff adjusted closes, one split or dividend rewrites that ticker's whole back-history and the diff lights up like the vendor lost the file.

store raw close and the adjustment factor in separate columns, diff them separately. then a restatement is one changed factor and a real data fix is one changed bar.

replies.author: Remarkable_Race5767
replies.body: That’s a really helpful distinction—thank you. We’ll keep the raw close and adjustment factor separate, then diff them independently. That way, a split or dividend adjustment appears as a changed factor, while an actual vendor data correction appears as a changed bar. This should make the audit trail much more reliable and prevent normal corporate-action adjustments from being mistaken for data errors.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: One that still slips past that split: vendors sometimes re-derive their whole factor history at once, so every row for a ticker changes factor on the same day. Looks like corruption, is actually housekeeping. Worth treating a factor change that spans the full history as a vendor event rather than a bad bar.
